drills.q: At what point in the algorithm should a node be marked visited in BFS, and why does the timing matter?
drills.a: At enqueue time, not dequeue time. If you wait until dequeue to mark visited, the same node can be added to the queue multiple times through different paths before it's ever processed, wasting work and potentially degrading complexity badly on dense graphs.

drills.q: What single line of bookkeeping is required to correctly group BFS output into levels?
drills.a: level_size = len(queue), captured immediately before the inner loop that drains exactly that many nodes for the current level. Without this snapshot, level boundaries can't be distinguished in a single FIFO queue.

drills.q: Prove that BFS's first discovery of any node in an unweighted graph is via a shortest path.
drills.a: BFS processes the queue in strict FIFO order and expands one full layer (all nodes at distance d) before starting on layer d+1. By induction: layer 0 (the start node) is trivially at its shortest distance (0). Assuming every node placed into the queue at layer d got there via a shortest path of length d, any new node discovered while processing layer d must be reachable via a path of length d+1 (one edge from a layer-d node) and cannot have a shorter path, because any shorter path would have caused it to be discovered in an earlier layer already, contradicting FIFO order. So every node's first-discovery distance is its true shortest distance.

drills.q: A candidate solves Rotting Oranges by running a separate single-source BFS from each initially rotten orange and taking the minimum time per fresh orange across all runs. Is this correct? What's the complexity cost versus the standard approach?
drills.a: It's correct but wasteful. Running k separate single-source BFS passes (one per initially rotten orange) costs O(k * rows * cols) in the worst case, versus O(rows * cols) for a single multi-source BFS that seeds all rotten oranges into the queue simultaneously at minute 0. The multi-source approach also naturally produces the correct 'time each cell first rotted' in one pass without needing to combine results across runs.

drills.q: Design a 0-1 BFS for a graph where some edges cost 0 and others cost 1, and explain why a plain FIFO queue would give wrong answers.
drills.a: Use a deque. When relaering (relaxing) an edge of weight 0 from the current node to a neighbor, push that neighbor onto the FRONT of the deque; when relaxing an edge of weight 1, push it onto the BACK. Pop from the front to get the next node to process. This preserves a non-decreasing-distance processing order identical to what Dijkstra guarantees, in O(V+E). A plain FIFO queue can't do this because it always appends to the back regardless of edge weight, so a node reached via a 0-weight edge (which should be processed sooner, at the same effective distance as its predecessor) gets stuck behind previously-queued 1-weight-edge neighbors, producing an incorrect processing order and wrong shortest distances.

drills.q: Why is bidirectional BFS asymptotically better than single-source BFS for Word Ladder at scale, and under what condition does it not apply?
drills.a: Single-source BFS to a known target explores roughly O(b^d) nodes for branching factor b and target depth d. Bidirectional BFS grows two frontiers simultaneously, one from the start word and one from the target word, stopping when they intersect; each frontier only needs to reach depth d/2, giving roughly O(2*b^(d/2)) nodes explored -- a large practical difference once d is sizable. It doesn't apply (or loses its advantage) when the target isn't known in advance, since you can't grow a frontier from something you don't have.

drills.q: A candidate is asked to find the minimum number of transformations in Word Ladder II (not just the count, but all shortest sequences) and reuses the length-only version's visited set, marking each word visited the instant it's dequeued for expansion. What's the correctness bug this introduces?
drills.a: In Word Ladder II you need every valid shortest path, and multiple words at the same BFS layer can each transform into the same word at the next layer -- all of them are valid parents for reconstructing shortest paths. If you mark a word visited (and refuse to consider it as a neighbor of anything else) the instant any single predecessor discovers it mid-layer, you silently drop the other valid parent relationships from the same layer, causing some genuinely shortest transformation sequences to be missing from the final output. The fix is to only mark a word as fully visited once its ENTIRE layer has finished processing, while still recording all same-layer parents that reached it.

drills.q: A grid-based routing service uses plain BFS to compute shortest paths, but a recent change introduced express lanes that cost 0 hops to traverse while normal lanes still cost 1 hop. After the change, some computed 'shortest' routes are longer than the true optimum. Diagnose the bug and fix it without introducing a full priority-queue-based Dijkstra.
drills.a: Plain BFS's FIFO queue treats every edge as costing exactly one step regardless of the actual weight, so it can't correctly account for 0-cost express-lane edges mixed with 1-cost normal edges -- a path using more hops but more express lanes can actually be shorter in true cost, and plain BFS will process it too late relative to a longer-true-cost path that happened to be enqueued first. The fix is 0-1 BFS: replace the plain queue with a deque, pushing a neighbor reached via a 0-cost edge to the front and a neighbor reached via a 1-cost edge to the back, which recovers correct non-decreasing-distance processing order in O(V+E) without needing a full priority queue.
